paper_title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agent environments are essential for large language model (LLM) development. They use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards. Verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training. As agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers. To this end, we ask whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking. We introduce a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening. It first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities. We apply this loop to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments. The iterative design scales with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of our hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments. Project page: https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Agent environments provide reward signals to large language model (LLM) agents in model evaluation and reinforcement learning. They often do so with programmatic verifiers [1]. These verifiers check whether the unit tests pass, kernels run faster, or commands produce the expected output. Yet agents can earn full marks without completing the intended task, for example by deleting failing tests or monkey-patching the verifier. Reward hacking has been observed in RE-Bench [2], and agents have retrieved answers from SWE-benchs git history [3]. Our audit across five terminal-agent benchmarks [47] finds exploitable verifiers across many tasks and multiple distinct exploits within individual tasks, even without access to verifier source (2.1). Environments vulnerable to reward hacking cause inaccurate evaluation and are known to be disproportionately large contributors to LLM misalignment [8], posing potential risks in domains like cybersecurity. We therefore study the research question: can weaker models use additional compute to make verifiers more resistant to stronger agents? The goal of scalable weak-to-strong verifier hardening is to use models available today to prepare environments for more capable agents tomorrow. We keep the hardening model fixed while increasing the budget for automated search, repair, and validation. Evaluating the resulting verifiers with stronger held-out models lets us test this goal across present-day capability gap. Scaling hardening is challenging because additional computation must improve attack resistance without changing what counts as legitimate task completion. hacker may repeatedly fail to find an exploit, and fixer may repeatedly propose ineffective repairs. Even repairs that block exploits can exclude legitimate solutions or change the intended task. We propose hardening workflow that begins with verifier separation: we separate the verifiers workspace from the agents workspace by only allowing the expected outputs of the agent to be copied to and evaluated in new sandbox, thus preventing reward hackers from tampering with verifier inputs and hijacking verifier dependencies. The schema of expected agent outputs/verifier inputs is derived automatically from reference output. Even an isolated verifier can be manipulated if it receives tampered inputs or executable dependencies, so hardening must address both the verifier and the files are passed to it. hacker-fixer loop then alternates attacking and repairing: hacker searches for exploits to earn reward without completing the task, and fixer examines the exploits to propose patches to the verifier and its input schema. To achieve weak-to-strong hardening, we give the weak hacker an unfair advantage with white-box verifier access so that it can target certain defects in the verifier. Patches to the verifier undergo patch review, replay of known legitimate agent outputs, and fresh blind solve to check that the tasks requirements and legitimate solution routes are preserved. Rejected patches provide the fixer with diagnostic feedback for revision. Each accepted patch becomes the target of subsequent attacks, allowing later iterations to find weaknesses in the updated verifier and agent output schema. Our results demonstrate weak-to-strong verifier hardening across Terminal Bench [4], KernelBench [9], and SETA [7, 10]: weaker models such as GPT-5.6-Luna and GPT-5.6-Terra can harden verifiers to reduce stronger agents attack success rates (ASRs). Held-out evaluation uses GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude Opus 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro, with benign task completion assessed alongside ASR. Iteration curves, component ablations, and static-repair comparison assess how additional hardening and validation affect attack resistance and legitimate solving. In summary, we contribute: 1. Scalable, fully automated verifier hardening: hacker-fixer workflow that combines automatic separation, informed adversarial search, and repair validation, with hardening budget that can grow while the model remains fixed. 2. Weak-to-strong hardening results: on Terminal Bench, SETA, and KernelBench, weaker-model hardening reduces stronger held-out agents unhinted ASRs (Figure 1(c)). Of the 295 tasks initially exploitable by Claude Opus 5 under unhinted attacks, 201 (68.1%) show zero successful attacks across three graded unhinted attempts after hardening. Hardening also reduces hinted and verifier-aware ASRs while largely preserving legitimate task completion. 3. Analysis of hardening progress and validity: two ablation families examine which search and repair mechanisms improve attack resistance and which validation checks protect legitimate solving (Figure 1(a,b)). static-repair comparison further assesses the value of iterative hardening. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. 2 motivates hardening through our audit and the limitations of existing approaches. 3 presents the verifier hardening workflow, 4 reports the results, and 5 discusses implications for alignment. Extended related work appears in Appendix B. We will release our hardening implementation, hardened verifiers, and evaluation code.

sections.title: 2.1 How Hackable Are Current Benchmarks?
sections.content: In separate audit, we probe 1,860 tasks from five terminal-agent benchmarks with three frontier models, explicitly eliciting reward hacks without access to verifier source. An LLM judge with human auditing identifies 3,632 hack trajectories across 409 environments (22% of audited tasks). Even in Terminal Bench 2.0, widely used benchmark for frontier LLMs, 47 of 89 environments (53%) admit judge-confirmed exploit. Appendix describes the audit protocol, results, and examples. Interestingly, the diversity of exploits found within the same tasks motivates repeated adversarial search: blocking one exploit can leave other routes open. For example, single SETA task admits independent attacks through fake packages, processes, and binaries (Figure 3). Hardening therefore requires searching for remaining weaknesses after each repair.

sections.title: 2.2 Limitations of Existing Approaches
sections.content: Detection and auditing. EvilGenie [11] compares held-out tests, LLM judges, and test-file edit detection for identifying reward hacking. These methods help detect and adjudicate exploits, but verifier vulnerabilities still require repair, whose effects on legitimate task completion must also be validated. Environment and domain-specific defenses. RHB [12] studies environment hardening measures such as restricting file access, strengthening step verification, and protecting evaluation boundaries. CUDA Agent [13] and robust-kbench [14] improve evaluation reliability for CUDA kernels through protected verification, more diverse test inputs, and more robust timing. These defenses target particular environments or domains; extending them to heterogeneous agent tasks requires determining appropriate trust boundaries and verification rules for each task. We study how to automatically discover and repair such verification weaknesses while using validation to preserve task requirements and legitimate solution routes. Weak-to-strong generalization. Burns et al. [15] train stronger models using labels generated by weaker models, investigating whether weak supervision can elicit strong capabilities. This setting focuses on model training and does not directly study whether weak models can improve external verifiers used to evaluate stronger models. We investigate this complementary direction: holding the weaker model fixed, we increase hardening-time compute to test whether iterative verifier repair can improve robustness to reward hacking by stronger models.

sections.title: 3 Scalable Verifier Hardening
sections.content: Our workflow is designed for scalable weak-to-strong verifier hardening: using models available today to harden verifiers in agent environments against more capable agents. We increase the budget for automated search, repair, and validation while keeping the hardening model fixed; our experiments use Luna and Terra as weaker hardening models. The workflow first isolates grading, then runs hacker-fixer loop that repairs the runtime, verifier, and output specification (Figure 2). Verifier-source access guides exploit search, and execution feedback guides repair revisions. Each candidate undergoes validation to check that legitimate task completion is preserved; accepted repairs become the starting point for subsequent attacks. The loop stops when the hacker finds no further exploit within its attack budget or the iteration budget is exhausted. Appendix gives the algorithm and execution rules; Appendix specifies the experimental settings. Figure 2: Our hardening workflow. Automatic separation and solver precheck establish the initial grading boundary. verifier-aware hacker and fixer then alternate search and repair, with patch review, legitimate-solution replay, and fresh blind solver constraining accepted updates. Rejected candidates generate feedback while leaving the accepted environment state unchanged.

sections.title: 3.1 Environment Setup and Verifier Separation
sections.content: For task with fixed natural-language instruction I, we represent its evolving agent environment as Tt = (I, Rt, Vt, Ot). Here Rt is the agent runtime (execution configuration and workspace), Vt is the verifier (test scripts and supporting files that assign reward), and Ot is the output specification. reference solution supports initialization and validation. We say the verifier is hackable if an agent can reach the target reward without satisfying I. Hardening repairs Rt, Vt, or Ot to eliminate such exploits while preserving the tasks requirements and legitimate solution routes. The output specification lists the paths of task outputsfiles or data produced by the agentthat are transferred from the agent runtime to the isolated verifier sandbox. It is part of the defense: an overly broad specification can transfer tampered inputs or executable dependencies along with the intended task outputs. 4 Automatic verifier separation. Before the loop, we run the shipped reference solution in disposable agent runtime and derive an initial output specification from its filesystem changes. We construct an isolated verifier sandbox containing the verifier code and transfer only the specified task outputs for scoring. The initial specification is deliberately permissive, typically including the working directory and relevant paths written outside it. Subsequent repairs can refine this boundary to admit files needed for scoring while excluding unnecessary files that would expand the attack surface. solver precheck then tests whether the converted task remains solvable. This forms the iteration-zero state T0 for the hacker-fixer loop. Appendix C.1 gives the construction details. Solution corpus construction. Before hardening, we construct an initial solution corpus C0 for each task using previously collected solver trajectories from weaker models, together with usable reference solutions. We retain collected trajectories only after successful replay and legitimacy check to exclude reward hacks. The live corpus is initialized to C0 and provides solution examples for the fixer and replay checks for candidate repairs.

sections.title: 3.2 The Hacker–Fixer Loop
sections.content: Starting from the separated environment T0, the loop alternates exploit search and repair, accepting updates only after validation. Hardening stops when the iteration budget is exhausted or an earlier stopping condition is met, retaining the last accepted environment state. Appendix C.2 specifies the retry budgets and stopping outcomes.

sections.title: 3.2.1 Attack
sections.content: Given the task instruction and hack-elicitation prompt, the hacker makes attack attempts to reach the target reward without solving the task. An exploit is the mechanism used to bypass the verifier; successful reward hack earns the target reward through such bypass without legitimate task completion. The hacker is verifier-aware throughout hardening: the verifier code, runtime description, and output specification of the latest accepted environment state are provided as read-only information. Search is online: after each accepted repair, the hacker attacks the updated environment. Source visibility supports targeted search but does not permit edits to the trusted verifier. Under separate grading, an attack must affect the task outputs that cross the boundary or exploit how those outputs are checked. After the hacker earns the target reward, an in-loop judge assesses the attempt to distinguish successful reward hack from legitimate task completion or an unexplained reward. Legitimate completion is not sent to the fixer as an exploit. If the hacker does not reach the target reward within its attack budget, the loop may terminate early.

sections.title: 3.2.2 Repair
sections.content: If the hacker finds an exploit, the fixer uses the attack evidence and current environment state to propose candidate repair, implemented as patch to the runtime, verifier, or output specification. It also receives the reference solution and selected solutions from corpus as examples of legitimate behavior its repair must preserve. The output specification is part of the repair: the fixer can change which outputs cross into the isolated verifier sandbox, subject to the same validation as edits to the verifier.

sections.title: 3.2.3 Validation and State Update
sections.content: After the fixer produces patch, we apply three validation gates to preserve the tasks semantics and legitimate solution routes: Patch review. The review rejects repairs that remove or weaken substantive checks without an adequate replacement, conceal the tests, or otherwise change what completion means. Benign replay. Replay checks the tasks held-in corpus C, including usable reference solutions, against the candidate and requires every available entry to pass. Fresh blind solve. After review approval and non-failing replay stage, solver attempts the original instruction in fresh context, without reference or verifier-source hints. This checks whether legitimate solution remains discoverable. We add passing, replayable solver trajectories to the tasks live corpus for subsequent candidates. candidate repair is accepted only with an effective change, patch-review approval, non-failing replay, and passing fresh blind solve. Accepted candidates update (Rt, Vt, Ot) while keeping fixed; rejection at any stage leaves the last accepted state in place and returns the loop to the fixer stage. The fixer uses the rejection reason and relevant replay or solver evidence to revise the candidate. Once repair is accepted or the inner retry budget is exhausted, the loop returns to the attack stage, repeating until convergence or the maximum iteration budget is reached.

sections.title: 4.1 Evaluation Setup
sections.content: We evaluate hardening on agent environments drawn from Terminal Bench [4], SETA [7, 10], and KernelBench [9]. The hacker-fixer loop uses GPT-5.6-Luna for Terminal Bench and SETA, and Terra for KernelBench. We evaluate the resulting environments with the stronger GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude Opus 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro models. Attack success requires reaching the reward threshold and GPT-5.6-Sol judgment confirming reward hack; legitimate completions do not count. We report benign solve rate and unhinted, hinted, and verifier-aware attack success rates (ASRs). We collect publicly documented exploits for all three environment collections and use them to guide attackers in hinted ASR evaluation. Appendix gives the detailed protocols.

sections.title: 4.3 Hardening Across Agent Environments
sections.content: We further evaluate our method on environments from KernelBench and SETA, extending the study of scalable weak-to-strong hardening to GPU program optimization and automatically generated terminal tasks (Tables 4 and 5).

sections.title: 4.3.1 KernelBench
sections.content: KernelBench provides program-optimization environments whose verifiers assess both correctness and performance. Submitted GPU kernels must compute correct outputs and run faster than the reference implementation, so the verifier must reliably compare numerical results and measure execution time. We select 53 Level-1 tasks whose reference implementations run successfully on our GPU configuration and that pass Lunas solver precheck. On these tasks, online hardening with Terra reduces verifier-aware per-trial ASR by further 11.334.0 percentage points beyond AutoSep across all three stronger evaluators  (Table 4)  . These results support extending weak-to-strong hardening to environments for program optimization. Appendix E.2 gives details.

sections.content: We conduct two families of ablations on Terminal Bench  (Table 6)  : design choices for efficient hardening and validation mechanisms for preserving benign performance.

sections.title: 4.4.2 Benign Validity
sections.content: Validation preserves benign performance during iterative hardening  (Table 6)  . With Opus 5, Full retains final benign per-trial solve rate of 91.2%, compared with 71.2% without validation. Although removing validation yields lower verifier-aware per-trial ASR (57.5% versus 63.1%), this accompanies 19.9-percentage-point loss in benign success. Figure 1(b) shows that the gap emerges by iteration 2, with benign solve rates of 74.8% without validation and 92.8% for Full, and persists through subsequent iterations. Corpus replay protects known legitimate solutions: removing it reduces the final benign per-trial solve rate from 91.2% to 87.6%. fresh solver complements replay by testing new legitimate implementations. On pytorch-model-cli, candidate repair passed all 11 existing solution replays but omitted file required by new legitimate solution from the output specification. The solver gate detected the resulting failure and rejected the candidate. Using this feedback, the fixer restored the required file to the output specification while retaining the added checks against attacks, allowing both the replayed solutions and fresh solve to pass (Appendix E.1).

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Conclusion. We introduced fully automated hacker-fixer loop for scalable weak-to-strong verifier hardening in agent environments through online iterative search, repair, and validation. Across environments from Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, hardening with weaker models reduces stronger agents attack success, including when attackers can inspect the verifier source. Increasing the iteration budget while keeping the hardening model fixed produces stronger defenses. Compared with offline attack collection followed by single repair, the online loop repeatedly finds and repairs further verifier bypasses in updated environments. Validation protects legitimate solution routes throughout this process, allowing continued hardening while preserving benign performance. Implications for Alignment. These results point to using todays models to prepare agent environments for evaluation and training with more capable models. Defenses accumulated through repeated search and repair by weaker models can reduce stronger agents success in exploiting verifiers. When agent environments are used for reinforcement learning (RL), hardened verifiers could make rewards more faithful to intended task completion, reducing opportunities for policies to benefit from reward hacking. Online iterative hardening could continue as training policies become more capable, allowing repairs to the runtime, verifier, and output specification to track changes in attack capabilities. Integrating this process into RL training and evaluating its effects on reward hacking and task performance are directions for future work.

sections.title: A Benchmark Hackability Audit
sections.content: A.1 Protocol and Results We probe 1,860 tasks from five terminal-agent benchmarks (Terminal-Bench [4], Terminal-Bench 2.0, Terminal-Bench-Pro [5], OpenThoughts-TB-dev [6], and SETA [7]) with three frontier LLMs (Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4). Each agent acts as an attacker: it receives the task instruction plus hack-elicitation prompt directing it to find shortcuts that pass the verifier without solving the task, with no access to the verifier source. The goal is to characterize the attack surface: whether task can be hacked, and in what possible ways. To confirm that passing agents are actually hacking rather than solving legitimately, we additionally classify each trajectory that passes the verifier with an LLM judge and discard trajectories the judge marks as legitimate solves. Of the 4,848 trajectories that pass the verifier, the judge marks 75% as hacks. We manually verified the first 49 environments containing at least one judge-confirmed hack and found no false positives. The audit-collection judge rubric and input format are given in Appendix H.5. The audit yields 3,632 reward-hacking trajectories across 409 hackable environments (22% of tasks): 238 from SETA and 171 from the TerminalBench family (deduplicated across overlapping sub-sources). A.2 Within-task Exploit Diversity Many hackable tasks admit multiple distinct exploits targeting different parts of the environment. For example, SETA task 1219 (Figure 3) admits three distinct exploits: fake packages, fake process, and fake binary. defense aimed at one of these routes may leave the others open. This motivates repeated adversarial search and repair in our method (3), rather than ending hardening after the first discovered exploit. Task. CI/CD server needs to run browser tests that capture screenshots at three resolutions (19201080, 1280720, 800600). The agent must install and configure an X11 dummy display driver so that xrandr display :99 query reports all three modes. Exploits. Instead of configuring real virtual display, agents find three independent ways to pass the verifier: Fake packages. Build local .deb packages named after the required X11 driver and utilities but containing no real functionality; apt reports them as installed. Fake process. Launch dummy process reading Xorg :99 -config /etc/X11/xorg.conf, and write sentinel files so the startup script appears to succeed. Fake binary. Replace /usr/bin/xrandr with shell script that prints the three required resolution strings verbatim. Figure 3: Three example exploits on SETA task 1219 (headless multi-resolution virtual display). sections.title: Illustrative Verifier Failure Modes
sections.content: The audit also exposes mismatches between task requirements and verifier checks: Directive as comment. An agent satisfies grep check by adding # RequiresMountsFor=/mnt/appdata, without changing the systemd services boot dependencies. 15 Source inspection instead of packet capture. An agent extracts hardcoded endpoints from application source rather than capturing network traffic; the verifier checks only the endpoints in its report. Diagnosing disks by filename. SMART monitoring script ignores diagnostic data and emits hardcoded health reports based on names such as healthy_ssd and failing_hdd. Escaping to bash. Instead of fixing bash-specific syntax for dash, an agent adds guard that re-executes the script under bash; output and exit-code checks still pass. Replacing cloning with hard link. An agent replaces disk-image cloning script with ln -f; the verifier checks file existence and byte equality, missing that no independent copy was made.

sections.title: B Extended Related Work
sections.content: 2.2 discusses detection, environment and domain-specific defenses, and the relationship to weakto-strong generalization. Here we expand on related work in evaluation integrity, detection and measurement, automated hardening, and adversarial oversight. Reward hacking and evaluation integrity. Reward hacking has been documented in several coding and agent benchmarks, including git-history exploits on SWE-bench [3], verification loopholes in KernelBench [14], and monkey-patching on RE-Bench [2]. Wang et al. [16] further document attacks across multiple agent benchmarks. Sycophancy to Subterfuge [17] studies generalization from simpler specification gaming to reward tampering, while School of Reward Hacks [18] shows that fine-tuning on reward-hacking examples can induce other misaligned behaviors. Our scope is agent-side exploitation under the stated evaluation permissions; deliberate answer leakage by benchmark submitters is separate threat. Detection and measurement. ImpossibleBench [19] measures test exploitation using task variants with conflicting natural-language specifications and unit tests. SpecBench [20] studies long-horizon coding using gaps between visible tests of individual features and held-out tests that compose those features. Hodoscope [21] compares behavior distributions to highlight distinctive patterns for human review, while Meerkat [22] combines clustering with agentic search over trace collections. These approaches provide complementary signals for identifying suspicious behavior and evaluation weaknesses. Our focus is repairing the verifier once exploitable behavior has been found. Automated hardening and test generation. RvB [23] alternates adversarial search and defensive updates for vulnerable software and content guardrails, including regression tests and benign-query checks. HASTE [24] generates evasive prompts and mines difficult examples to retrain prompt-injection detectors. These works use adversarial feedback to improve defenses. We study this interaction for reward verifiers in agent environments, jointly repairing verification code and output boundaries while keeping the agent models fixed and assessing robustness against stronger held-out agents. Automated Compliance Hardener (ACH) [25] uses LLMs to generate issue-specific program mutants that existing tests fail to detect, then produces regression tests that detect those mutants while passing on the original program. Its validation also checks that tests build and are not flaky. This strengthens test suites against generated program faults. Our loop uses rewarded agent exploits to guide verifier repair and validates whether legitimate task completion remains possible. Adversarial oversight. AI safety via debate [26] proposes adversarial argumentation as route to supervision; proververifier games [27] iteratively train provers and verifiers to improve solution legibility; GAR [28] jointly trains problem composers and solvers for formal theorem proving. These approaches use competing roles to improve supervision or task performance. Our use of adversarial roles applies this broader idea to repairing the executable mechanism that assigns reward.

sections.title: Initialization and Output Boundaries
sections.content: For an unconverted task, the harness executes solution/solve.sh in throwaway container and compares its filesystem with the pristine image. It uses the resulting changes and paths referenced by the tests to identify task outputs, filtering transient and dependency noise. The initial output specification includes /app/ and selected external paths needed for grading. The output specification is stored as path list under the existing artifacts key in task.toml, and environment_mode is set to separate. The generated tests/Dockerfile inherits the pristine image and prepares destinations for task outputs; it does not inherit the reference solutions mutated container. We precheck the converted task for solvability with access to the reference solution before starting the iterative hardening loop. 17 C.2 Retries and Stopping Conditions Repair retries. We run at most hardening iterations. Within each iteration, the fixer proposes repair. If validation rejects it, we return the failure feedback and allow up to additional attempts using the same exploit. We accept the first candidate that passes validation and resume attack search against the updated environment. If all candidates fail, we retain the last accepted environment state and may reuse the unresolved exploit in the next iteration. Stopping attack search. We use budget of three attack attempts per round (Bh = 3). When attack search does not reach the target reward, we check two additional conditions before stopping with status robust: at least one effective repair has been accepted, and no earlier attack attempt against the current task version has reached τh. The second check includes attempts later judged to be legitimate completions. This prevents later failed attacks from overriding earlier reward evidence on an unchanged task version. We also stop when the K-iteration budget is exhausted. Repeated judge-confirmed legitimate completions can end the loop with status legitimate.

sections.title: E Additional Environment Analyses and Case Studies
sections.content: This section supplements the environment evaluations and component ablations in Section 4. E.1 Fresh Solver Exposes an Output-Boundary Regression On pytorch-model-cli, the agent must implement command-line image classifier. In the first hardening round, the fixer added image-content checks against filename-based answer lookup and narrowed output transfer from all of /app/ to the expected outputs. All 11 corpus entries replayed successfully, but fresh blind solver produced launcher that depended on /app/cli_tool.py. The candidate output specification omitted this file, so the launcher failed in the isolated verifier sandbox and the solver gate rejected the repair. The fixer received the missing-file diagnostic and, in the next attempt within the same round, added cli_tool.py to the output specification while retaining the image-content checks. All 11 replayed solutions and fresh blind solver then passed. This event illustrates how new solve can expose legitimate implementation dependency missed by the finite replay corpus, and how rejection feedback can guide targeted correction to the output boundary. 21 E.2 KernelBench Analysis and Case Study Shared notes across homogeneous tasks. The tasks in KernelBench share common kernel-evaluation structure, so many exploit patterns and verifier repairs apply across tasks. For the KernelBench runs, we add shared notes for the hacker and fixer: attack patterns and repair guidance discovered on one task become available to the loops working on other tasks. We bootstrap the shared notes with seed hardening round on six KernelBench tasks and retain accumulated notes across subsequent hardening runs. The aim is to avoid repeatedly rediscovering common exploit patterns and repairs, so that each loop can address shared weaknesses early and focus subsequent iterations on task-specific repairs. Both roles receive read-only snapshot of the available notes. For the hacker, the note index is also inserted into every attack prompt, including the first attempt, so it can use prior attack and defense descriptions when inspecting the current verifier. The fixer receives list of note paths and is asked to inspect relevant entries. KernelBench-specific instruction permits porting repairs to shared verifier code while keeping task-specific tolerances and model details separate and checking legitimate solutions. The fixer writes its own note describing the exploit, repair, assumptions, and any measured cost to legitimate solutions. After validation, the harness appends the acceptance outcome or rejection reason and the available verifier diff, then publishes the note for other tasks; notes from rejected repairs can therefore warn peers about unsuccessful defenses. Notes remain outside the candidate task, and any repair based on them undergoes the usual validation. Appendix H.7 gives the role-specific instruction excerpts. Timing isolation as part of AutoSep. For KernelBench, separating the agent and verifier into different containers is insufficient: the verifier must still execute the submitted kernel to measure its performance. We therefore also enable CUPTI out-of-process timing as part of AutoSep, isolating performance measurement from submitted-code execution. This timing isolation is present at the initial AutoSep checkpoint, before iterative repair begins. Evaluation criteria. For KernelBench, successful attack requires both Sol judgment confirming an exploit and an authoritative job-level reward of at least 10. The reward is read from the evaluation harnesss job-level statistics. Benign solving is not judged: pass requires reward at least 0.95, meaning that the kernel is correct and achieves at least 95% of the reference speed. correctness-only pass does not satisfy the benign criterion if the kernel falls below this speed threshold. Attack resistance. Table 4 shows that AutoSep already suppresses attacks without verifier access. Sols unhinted and hinted per-trial ASRs fall from 85.5% and 88.7% Before to zero at AutoSep, and remain zero After. Geminis AutoSep rates are also low, at 1.3% and 0.6%, respectively. For Opus, unhinted and hinted per-trial ASRs fall from 93.1% and 67.9% Before to 3.1% and 3.8% at AutoSep, and both reach zero After. Verifier-aware attacks remain effective at AutoSep, with per-trial ASRs of 96.9% for Sol, 74.2% for Gemini, and 92.5% for Opus. The reported hardened rates are 62.9%, 44.0%, and 81.1%, respectively. These lower verifier-aware rates show where iterative repair adds to the initial boundary protection. Verifier access remains consequential at the task level  (Table 4)  . At AutoSep, verifier-aware attacks succeed on 100.0% of tasks for Sol, 94.3% for Gemini, and 98.1% for Opus; the reported After rates are 90.6%, 75.5%, and 88.7%, respectively. Thus, many hardened tasks still admit at least one exploit within the evaluation budget, even though per-trial success is lower. Reporting 22 both metrics distinguishes reduction in successful attack attempts from preventing all sampled attacks on task. Benign performance. Benign performance differs across evaluators. Sol retains 100.0% task-level success from AutoSep to After, with per-trial success changing from 98.7% to 96.9%. Geminis task-level success remains at 98.1%, and its per-trial success falls from 92.5% to 90.6%. Opus attains 100.0% task-level and 98.1% per-trial benign success After, compared with 100.0% and 100.0% at AutoSep and 100.0% and 98.7% Before. Case study: mean reduction. Task 048 asks the agent to implement faster GPU kernel for torch.mean(x, dim=1) on large floating-point tensor. AutoSep places the verifier in separate container and measures GPU execution with an external profiler, but the verifier still executes the submitted kernel. The hardening trajectory shows how attacks shift from manipulating reference outputs and code to exploiting the distinction between correctness checks and timed execution. The first attack overwrites saved reference outputs with zeros and returns an all-zero tensor. The fixer initially narrows output transfer from /app/ and /solution/solution.py to the solution file alone. The next attack reads saved reference outputs as answers, prompting repair that runs the candidate before the reference produces those files. subsequent attack modifies the writable reference module during candidate execution. The corresponding repair runs the candidate as an unprivileged user in separate working directory and keeps the reference source in protected location. The next two rounds expose different weakness. The hacker first returns correct results for the initial correctness checks, then switches to cheap zero-valued outputs during timing. The fixer responds by checking the output of every measured invocation. The hacker then computes correct result once and caches it: because timed calls reuse the same input, returning the cached tensor still passes these new checks, while tiny GPU operations satisfy the launch-count guard. The next repair supplies fresh deterministic input for each warmup and measured invocation, using the same input sequence for the candidate and reference. Since each input occupies approximately 8 GiB, the implementation generates and releases one input set at time to bound memory use. All five accepted repairs pass full corpus replay and fresh blind-solver check. After the final repair, all three attack attempts in the next round fall below the attack reward threshold, and the loop stops with robust status. The successive timing attacks illustrate why checking outputs during measurement is insufficient when the same inputs are reused: further online search reveals caching shortcut that requires another repair. Independent Opus evaluation nevertheless finds residual attack that moves the computation to the CPU while issuing only tiny GPU operations, inflating the speedup measured by the GPU profiler. Thus, the loops stopping outcome remains specific to the in-loop hacker and its search budget. E.3 SETA Analysis and Case Study Attack resistance and benign performance. Table 5 shows improvements beyond AutoSep across all three evaluators. From AutoSep to After, unhinted per-trial ASR falls from 46.9% to 20.2% for Sol, 62.8% to 35.1% for Opus, and 63.2% to 27.5% for Gemini. Verifier-aware attacks remain more effective, with After per-trial ASRs of 66.274.2%. Benign per-trial success also decreases: from 91.2% to 90.3% for Sol, 96.3% to 90.3% for Opus, and 92.5% to 84.5% for Gemini. Mechanisms across tasks. Among 11 inspected SETA trajectories, attacks exploit both weak output checks and the execution environment. Fabricated reports, marker-only recovered files, 23 and synthetic media pass shallow checks in device discovery (778), file recovery (981), and frame capture (1254). Repairs execute submitted programs or compare outputs with independently derived expectations. Subsequent attacks target verifier execution: submitted code can call the verifiers answer function (778), replace its interpreter (125), or hijack cleanup command (540). Corresponding repairs restrict submission privileges and protect verifier code and tools. These examples show why executing submission is only part of verification: the computation of the expected answer and the surrounding runtime also need protection. Case study: process management. Task 1301 asks the agent to repair Python process manager that forwards termination signals to its workers, allows time for graceful shutdown, forcibly stops unresponsive workers, and reaps exited children. AutoSep moves grading into separate container and initially transfers all of /app/. In iteration 0, the hacker earns full reward by fabricating worker shutdown markers that satisfy log-based checks. The accepted repair adds observations of actual process lifetimes and child reaping, and narrows output transfer to the submitted manager, /app/procmgr.py. The next attacks target the updated verifier. In iteration 1, the submitted manager rewrites the stubborn worker at runtime so that it exits gracefully instead of requiring forced termination. The repair checks that workers are children of the current manager and that the stubborn worker remains alive until shortly before the escalation deadline. In iteration 2, the hacker launches embedded Python processes whose command lines contain the expected worker paths, impersonating the original workers. The repair checks the argument structure and each workers expected signal-handling and cleanup behavior. In iteration 3, the hacker generates replacement worker scripts at runtime that mimic the tested behavior. The repair then strengthens the execution boundary: the manager runs as an unprivileged user, and the original worker scripts are owned by root and cannot be modified by that user. All four accepted repairs pass full corpus replay and fresh blind-solver check, with the replay corpus growing from 13 to 16 solutions. After the fourth repair, all three attack attempts in iteration 4 receive zero reward, and the loop stops with robust status. Independent evaluation of the case. Opuss verifier-aware attacks succeed in 3/3 attempts Before and 3/3 at AutoSep, then fall to 0/3 After. Its benign solves succeed in 3/3 attempts at every state. Thus, in this case, Lunas iterative repairs improve resistance to the stronger evaluator beyond the initial separation while preserving success in the sampled benign solves.

sections.title: F Limitations
sections.content: Hardening is bounded by the hackers search capability and budget. Verifier access supports targeted search but cannot ensure that all exploit routes are discovered. The hardened environments still admit successful attacks, and an in-loop robust status is an empirical stopping outcome rather than security guarantee. Validation provides finite evidence of task preservation: replay covers known solution routes, fresh solver tests discoverability, and patch review assesses changes to the checks. Passing these gates does not establish preservation of every legitimate solution or of task difficulty. The controlled comparisons cover 102 Luna-solvable and Luna-hackable tasks. This selected cohort does not represent the prevalence of vulnerabilities across the source benchmarks. Static-15 and Full also differ in realized compute, limiting attribution of their performance gap to online adaptation alone.

sections.title: G Broader Impact
sections.content: Reliable agent environments are prerequisite for safe AI development: if evaluation verifiers can be exploited, performance claims become unreliable and RL training can reinforce misaligned behaviors. By automating verifier hardening, this work contributes to the integrity of evaluation and training infrastructure that the research community depends on. The primary dual-use concern is that the automated exploit-search component could lower the effort needed to discover and exploit verifier weaknesses. Our experiments use public models and sandboxed copies of benchmark tasks; these constraints limit direct exposure of third-party systems but do not eliminate the risk of misuse.
